items.followUp: Define the internal energy of a body.

rubric.why: Identifies the two forms of molecular energy that make up internal energy.
rubric.description: Internal energy includes kinetic energy and potential energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both forms of energy.

rubric.why: Clarifies that the energies are those of the body's molecules.
rubric.description: The kinetic and potential energies belong to the molecules of the body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating both energies to the body's molecules.

modelAnswer: The internal energy of a body is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules.

items.followUp: Write four differences between distance and displacement.

rubric.why: Distinguishes mass by what it measures and weight as a gravitational force.
rubric.description: Mass is the amount of matter in a body; weight is the gravitational force acting on it.

rubric.why: Distinguishes mass as scalar and weight as vector.
rubric.description: Mass is a scalar quantity; weight is a vector quantity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both quantities correctly.

rubric.why: Gives the correct SI units for mass and weight.
rubric.description: Mass is measured in kilograms (kg); weight is measured in newtons (N).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both correct SI units.

rubric.why: States that mass is location-independent while weight varies with gravitational field strength.
rubric.description: Mass remains constant with location; weight changes when gravitational field strength changes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this correct comparison.

modelAnswer: Mass is the amount of matter in a body; weight is the gravitational force acting on it.
Mass is a scalar quantity; weight is a vector quantity.
The SI unit of mass is kilogram (kg); the SI unit of weight is newton (N).
Mass remains constant with location; weight changes when gravitational field strength changes.

items.followUp: Define base and derived quantities and give one example of each.

accept: not defined in terms of other quantities
rubric.why: Defines a base quantity and gives a valid example.
rubric.description: A base quantity is independent and is not defined in terms of other quantities; length is one example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition and a correct base-quantity example.

rubric.why: Defines a derived quantity and gives a valid example.
rubric.description: A derived quantity is obtained by combining base quantities; speed is one example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition and a correct derived-quantity example.

modelAnswer: Base quantities are independent quantities that are not defined in terms of other quantities; length is an example.
Derived quantities are obtained by combining base quantities; speed is an example.

items.followUp: Estimate the number of seconds in 12 years.

rubric.why: Identifies the given time and sets up the conversion from years to seconds.
rubric.description: Uses 14 years and converts using 365 days per year, 24 hours per day, 60 minutes per hour and 60 seconds per minute.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the given time and a valid conversion setup.

rubric.why: Gives the estimated number of seconds with its unit.
rubric.description: The estimated time is approximately 4.4 × 10⁸ s.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct estimated answer with the unit.

modelAnswer: Using 1 year = 365 days, 1 day = 24 h, 1 h = 60 min and 1 min = 60 s
